title: Device window 1: put the motion listener on the watch, then wear it for 24 hours
description:
## Why this needs you (please confirm this is accurate)
The watch listener (`msense`, in my-bangle at commit 78c796d) passes its tests in Node, and that is as far as I can take it alone. Putting it on the watch needs three things only you can do: turn the phone's Bluetooth off, set the watch connectable, and click Chrome's device chooser. Two of the measurements also need your wrist: I cannot feel whether the watch buzzed.

## Steps
Allow about 30 minutes at the Mac, with the watch on your wrist and a Claude session open in the mobile-motion-sensor repo. This follows procedure A then B in my-bangle `docs/troubleshooting.md`; nothing is unpaired and the watch is not rebooted.

1. Tell the agent "device window 1 for mobile-motion-sensor". It opens https://banglejs.com/apps/ in a tab of its own. Do not use a tab you opened.
2. Turn Bluetooth OFF on the phone.
3. On the watch: Settings, Bluetooth, Make Connectable. Leave the "Stay Connectable?" prompt on screen.
4. In the agent's tab, click Connect and pick the watch in Chrome's chooser. This is the only click.
5. Stay nearby for about 20 minutes. The agent snapshots the watch, writes `msense.boot.js`, reads it back, then measures: whether the scan restarts after each app switch and how long it is off, memory in every app, and the buzz test. For the buzz test it will ask you three times, "did you feel that?": once normally, once with quiet mode on, once with Vibration off. It puts both settings back.
6. When the agent says it is finished and has closed its tab: on the watch answer YES to "Stay Connectable?", then turn the phone's Bluetooth back on. Check Gadgetbridge reconnects by itself, with no pairing prompt.
7. Wear the watch as usual for at least 24 hours. It is now scanning 40 ms in every second, which is the first battery pattern. Do not charge it during that time if you can avoid it; if you do, note when.
8. During those 24 hours, send yourself one test notification and see whether it reaches the watch.
9. Add a note to this issue (`bd note <this-id> "..."`): did Gadgetbridge reconnect cleanly, did the test notification arrive, any buzz you did not expect, and any charging times. Then close it.

## What unblocks me when this returns
The closed issue and its note. At the next window I read `msense.log` and the widminbat hourly log off the watch, which gives the battery drain for the first scan pattern and whether scanning ran alongside Gadgetbridge, and I set the next pattern. If Gadgetbridge did not reconnect or notifications stopped, say so in the note and I take the listener off before anything else.

title: Which Bluetooth advertiser may I use for early watch measurements?
description:
## Why this needs you (please confirm this is accurate)
Some watch-side measurements can start before the parts arrive, but one of them (radio latency and loss) needs a Bluetooth advertiser whose packets I can change at a known moment. Only you know what hardware is lying around, and one of the candidates is your Home Assistant Pi, which I will not touch without being told to. I ruled out the Mac: macOS and Chrome cannot advertise manufacturer data.

## Question
Which controllable Bluetooth advertiser, if any, should I use for the watch's latency and loss measurements before the Puck arrives?

Options considered:
- A: A spare ESP32 board on USB to this Mac — I write a small sketch that advertises the protocol's payload and changes the counter on command, so timing is exact. Needs a board that is not doing another job.
- B: nRF Connect on your Android phone — free, no hardware, but you tap to change the packet, Android chooses the advertising interval, and the phone is also the Gadgetbridge host. Good for a rough check, poor for 50 timed trials.
- C: The Pi 5 that runs Home Assistant — it can advertise anything, but its Bluetooth adapter serves Home Assistant, and I would be changing a working system for a test.
- D: Nothing. Wait for the Puck and run latency and loss then.
Recommendation: A if you have a spare ESP32, otherwise D. The other early measurements (scan across app switches, scan alongside Gadgetbridge, memory, battery drain) do not need a special advertiser and go ahead either way in the next watch device window.

Answer by replying in a `bd note` on this issue (or editing this
description), then bounce it back with H. Close instead if the question is moot.

## What unblocks me when this returns
The letter. A: tell me which board and that it is plugged in, and I write the sketch and schedule the trials. B: I write you a short runbook for nRF Connect. C: I ask you which adapter Home Assistant uses before touching anything. D: the latency issue (mobile-motion-sensor-xx0) waits for the Puck development build.

## Why this needs you (please confirm this is accurate)
The project needs parts, and buying them takes your Adafruit account and your money. I cannot place an order. I checked the list in the brief (docs/brief-2026-11-16.md, "Hardware on order") against the bench plan and found nothing missing for the plan as written, so this should be the only order. Two things to look at before you pay are in step 2.

## Steps
1. Open your list, motion-sensor-order.md, and the Adafruit cart. The brief's list is: Puck.js v2 (3372) x1, BS412 PIR (4666) x2, BL412 PIR (4667) x2, mini PIR with header (4871) x1, 100 uF capacitors (2193) x1 pack, 0.1 uF capacitors (753) x1 pack, male/male jumper wires 3 in (1956) x1 pack, tiny breadboard (65) x1, CR2032 cells (654) x2.
2. Before paying, decide two things:
   - A second Puck.js (3372). It is optional. With one, the second-sensor requirement is proven on real hardware and I get a second radio for the "a stranger cannot connect" test. Without one, I prove the second sensor with a simulated broadcast and say so.
   - Look at the product photos for 4666 and 4667. If the four legs look too close together or too thick for a breadboard, nothing extra is needed: you would solder them to cut jumper wires, and the pack of 20 covers it. I only want you to know before the bench session.
3. Place the order.
4. Add a note to this issue (`bd note <this-id> "..."`) with:
   - the order date and expected arrival
   - whether you added the second Puck
   - which of these you have: a soldering iron, a multimeter with a microamp range, calipers, a 3D printer. The brief assumes all four and nobody has confirmed them. The microamp range matters most: without it the Puck's current cannot be measured.
5. Close this issue when the parts are in your hands, not when the order is placed. Everything on the bench is blocked on it.

## What unblocks me when this returns
The parts on your desk, and the note from step 4. A closed issue tells me to prepare the first bench session: unbox and power the Puck, read the 3V pad, run both recovery paths, and prove I can program it from a browser tab. If a tool is missing I will change the affected bench step instead of asking for a second order.

title: Proof of concept: Puck, one PIR on jumper wires, watch buzzes on a walk-past
description:
## Why this needs you (please confirm this is accurate)
This is the proof of concept: one Puck, one PIR, jumper wires, and the watch buzzes when you walk past. No soldering, no meter, nothing cut. The code is written and passes its tests in Node, but none of it has run on a device, and getting it onto the Puck and the watch takes clicks on Chrome's device chooser, the phone's Bluetooth switch and the watch's menu, which are yours. Wiring the sensor takes hands.

The Puck's packaging and LED behaviour below come from Espruino's page, and the PIR's leg numbering from my reading of the BS412 datasheet drawing (page 3). Neither has been checked on the real part. If something looks different, say what you see.

## Steps
About 30 to 45 minutes at the Mac with a Claude session open in the mobile-motion-sensor repo, watch on your wrist. Have ready: one Puck.js, one BS412 (Adafruit 4666), the tiny breadboard, four jumper wires. Say "proof of concept" to start.

**Part 1: the Puck's button buzzes the watch (no wiring)**

1. Peel the silicone cover off the Puck and tip the board out. Pull out the clear plastic tab under the coin cell, if there is one. Seat the cell without pressing the button beside it. Expect one brief red flash.
2. The agent opens a Chrome tab of its own. When it asks, click Connect in that tab and pick "Puck.js" plus four characters in the chooser. The agent loads a test program where the button stands in for the PIR. Expect red, green and blue to flash together when it starts.
3. Turn Bluetooth OFF on the phone. On the watch: Settings, Bluetooth, Make Connectable, and leave the "Stay Connectable?" prompt on screen.
4. The agent opens a second tab (https://banglejs.com/apps/). Click Connect there and pick the watch in the chooser. The agent puts the listener on the watch and says when it is done.
5. Press the Puck's button once, briefly. Expect a green flash: armed. Wait 3 seconds.
6. Press it again. Expect a short blue blink on the Puck and **a buzz on the watch**. Press a few more times, a few seconds apart. Tell the agent what you felt.

If step 6 buzzes, the radio and the watch are proven. If the Puck blinks blue and the watch stays quiet, tell the agent and stop here: that is the finding.

**Part 2: the PIR does it**

7. The agent loads the PIR program onto the Puck (one more chooser click if it asks).
8. Gently spread the BS412's four legs so each can go in its **own breadboard row**, and push them in. Seated straight, two of them would share a row, which is why they need spreading.
9. Work out which leg is which. Hold the sensor with the **legs pointing at you** and the small metal tab on the rim at the **upper right**. Then: top leg is 1, right is 2, bottom is 3, left is 4. The tab sits between legs 1 and 2.
10. Four jumper wires:
    - leg 1's row to leg 2's row (on the breadboard)
    - leg 1's row to the Puck's **GND** hole
    - leg 3's row to the Puck's **D2** hole
    - leg 4's row to the Puck's **D1** hole
    At the Puck, push the jumper's pin through the hole and let the wire lean so the pin presses on the hole's edge. Do not use the 3V hole. Tell the agent when it is wired.
11. Point the sensor's window away from you, across where you will walk. Press the Puck's button once: green flash, armed. **Keep still and out of its view for 30 seconds** while the sensor settles.
12. Walk across its view. Expect a blue blink on the Puck and a buzz on the watch. Repeat a few times, at least 5 seconds apart, and tell the agent what happened each time.

If nothing happens in step 12: nudge the three pins at the Puck, since leaning contacts are the likeliest fault, and try again. If the blue blink never comes, legs 3 and 4 may be the other way round from my reading of the drawing: swap the D1 and D2 wires at the Puck and repeat steps 11 and 12. I do not expect a swapped sensor to be damaged at coin-cell power, but I cannot promise it.

**Closing**

13. When the agent says it has closed its tabs: answer YES to "Stay Connectable?" on the watch, then turn the phone's Bluetooth back on. Check Gadgetbridge reconnects by itself.
14. Close this issue, or add a note saying which step you stopped at (`bd note mobile-motion-sensor-maf "..."`).

## What unblocks me when this returns
Whether the watch buzzed on the button (step 6) and on a walk-past (step 12), and anything that did not match the steps. I record it as the first measured result in the repo and correct the wiring notes from what the real sensor did. What to do after a working proof is your call.

title: Confirm two assumptions and two defaults that need no measurements
description:
## Why this needs you (please confirm this is accurate)
The brief of 2026-11-16 carries two assumptions marked "not confirmed by the owner" and two proposed defaults that need no measurements. All four shape the design from the first line of code, and they are yours to decide, not mine. The decisions that do need numbers (watch battery cost, lost-sensor timing, repeat alerts, arming confirmation) are not here; they come later with the measurements.

## Question
Do you accept all four of these, or which would you change?

1. Gadgetbridge must keep delivering phone notifications while the sensor is in use.
2. The phone is not in the alert path. A phone relay is a last resort only.
3. Forged or replayed broadcasts: accept the risk and document it. Anyone in Bluetooth range with the right tool could make your watch buzz or hide a lost sensor until its next heartbeat. They cannot reprogram the sensor. Details in docs/protocol.md, "Security".
4. You design the case, from dimensions I supply after the range test.

Options considered:
- A: Yes to all four — the design proceeds as drafted in docs/protocol.md.
- B: Change one or more — say which. A no on 3 means a shared key on the sensor and the watch, stored in 1Password, and a longer packet. A no on 1 or 2 reopens the architecture choice.
Recommendation: A. On 3, the sensor is a doorbell, not a lock, and a key adds a credential to manage on a device with no screen.

Answer by replying in a `bd note` on this issue (or editing this
description), then bounce it back with H. Close instead if the question is moot.

## What unblocks me when this returns
"All yes", or the numbers you would change with what you want instead. All yes: I record the four as owner decisions dated to your answer, in the changelog and docs/protocol.md. Anything else: I rework the affected part before writing firmware that depends on it.
